lesson.title: Why Python Stops Early: Short Circuit Evaluation
lesson.summary: Python evaluates and and or from left to right and stops as soon as the final result is guaranteed, a behavior called short circuit evaluation that both saves work and enables safe guard conditions.
lesson.body:
and and or do not necessarily evaluate both of their sides. Python evaluates the left side of an and expression first; if that left side is False, the entire and expression is already guaranteed to be False no matter what the right side turns out to be, since and requires both sides to be True. Python takes advantage of this and skips evaluating the right side entirely in that case. The same idea applies to or in reverse: Python evaluates the left side first, and if it is True, the whole or expression is already guaranteed to be True, so the right side is never evaluated. This behavior is called short circuit evaluation, because it lets Python cut the circuit short once the answer is already settled.

This is not just an efficiency trick, though it is that too. Short circuit evaluation is what makes a common and important pattern safe: guarding a risky operation behind a condition that must be checked first, so the risky part only runs once safety has already been confirmed.

Trace this example carefully:

x = 0
safe = x != 0 and (10 / x) > 1
print(safe)

Python evaluates the left side first, x != 0, substituting 0 for x, which gives 0 != 0, a False result. Because the left side of and is already False, and can never become True by evaluating the right side, so Python skips (10 / x) > 1 entirely and never attempts the division. safe is bound directly to False. If Python evaluated both sides regardless of the left result, this line would raise a ZeroDivisionError instead of quietly producing False, since dividing by zero is not allowed.

This same guard pattern appears constantly with lists as well: checking i < len(my_list) and my_list[i] == target relies on short circuit evaluation to avoid an IndexError, since the length check on the left must fail first, before Python ever attempts to look up my_list[i], whenever i is out of range. Understanding short circuit evaluation also clarifies a subtler point covered in the next section: and and or in Python do not always return a plain True or False. They actually return whichever operand's value decided the outcome, which becomes important once truthiness and falsiness enter the picture.

or short circuits in the mirror image situation: user_input or fetch_default_from_database() only calls the potentially slow database function if user_input is falsy, skipping that costly work entirely whenever a usable value is already available. This same left to right, stop as soon as possible behavior is why the order of conditions in an and or or expression can matter for performance as well as correctness: placing a cheap, frequently false condition before an expensive one in an and expression, or a cheap, frequently true condition before an expensive one in an or expression, lets short circuit evaluation skip the expensive check as often as possible.
